stories.headline: Cut National Insurance for under-25s to create jobs, Milburn report to say
stories.claim: Alan Milburn's youth unemployment review will urge phased cuts to employer National Insurance for 21-24-year-olds and tighter benefit rules for under-25s.
stories.summary: A major independent review led by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will recommend gradually cutting employer National Insurance for workers aged 21 to 24, starting with retail and hospitality, to tackle youth unemployment. The report, due for publication on Tuesday, comes after a year of work and is framed around the roughly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training (Neets). Milburn argues the government spends £22bn a year supporting economically inactive young people and proposes stricter benefit rules, including ending the health element of Universal Credit and Pip for under-25s. The proposals would also test Chancellor John Healey's fiscal room and the Labour government's welfare agenda.
key_points: The review will propose cutting employer NI for 21-24-year-olds over five years, starting with retail and hospitality, which employ 37% of 16-24-year-olds.
Milburn wants the existing NI threshold for 21-24-year-olds doubled from £5,000 to £10,000, but only when fiscal conditions allow.
An immediate scrapping of NI for that age group would cost £5.1bn, according to the Resolution Foundation.
Under-25s would lose eligibility for the health element of Universal Credit and Pip, and a legal job guarantee would tie benefits to taking up help.
Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the subsidised jobs guarantee would be extended to 18-24-year-olds on Universal Credit after 12 months, helping over 90,000 people by March 2029.
The Conservatives, through Helen Whately, want employer NI halved, while Milburn backed slowing the convergence of youth minimum wage rates.
stories.market_take: Proposed NI cuts would mainly affect retail and hospitality employers, but the review is advisory and any cut depends on fiscal room.

stories.headline: Britain could face Ireland genocide claim under new definition
stories.claim: UK experts warn a looser ICJ definition of genocide could expose Britain to legal claims, ahead of a Rohingya ruling this week.
stories.summary: Britain could face genocide claims over its past and present conduct, from the Irish potato famine to Kenya's Mau Mau suppression, if the International Court of Justice loosens the legal test for genocide. A Policy Exchange report published on Sunday, written with former ambassador Sir John Jenkins, international lawyer Dr Tom Grant and Air Marshal Edward Stringer, warns that a lower bar could let adversaries seek rulings against British ministers, officials and military alliances. The ICJ is due to rule this week on whether Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya amounts to genocide, and some states and campaign groups are pressing for the threshold to be lowered to a 'reasonable inference' of intent. The current standard, applied in cases such as Srebrenica, requires that genocidal intent be the only reasonable explanation for a state's conduct. The report also includes forewords from former Ukrainian foreign minister Dmytro Kuleba and Aharon Barak, who argue that intent must remain a high bar.
key_points: Policy Exchange warns that lowering the ICJ's threshold for genocide could expose British ministers, officials and the military to legal claims.

stories.headline: Scientists Discover New Deep-Sea Shark Species Hiding In Plain Sight
stories.claim: Indian scientists have formally identified a new deep-sea bramble shark species, Echinorhinus roinee, off Kerala.
stories.summary: Indian scientists have formally named a new deep-sea shark species, Echinorhinus roinee, after specimens long mistaken for the Atlantic bramble shark were caught off India's south-western coast. The roughly three-metre animals, with thorn-like dermal denticles, had been landed at fishing harbours such as Sakthikulangara in Kerala for years. Researchers from the Zoological Survey of India and the ICAR-Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute found anatomical differences, and DNA analysis showed the Indian sharks form a distinct evolutionary lineage separate from both the Atlantic and Pacific bramble sharks. Very little is known about the species' biology, but bramble sharks are generally thought to grow slowly and mature late, which makes the discovery a reminder of how much of the deep ocean remains poorly studied.
key_points: The new species, Echinorhinus roinee, is known as the Indian bramble shark.
Specimens were previously assumed to be Atlantic bramble sharks and were landed in Kerala for years.

stories.headline: Vulcan rocket fails on first Amazon Leo launch, losing 40 satellites and likely grounding rocket
stories.claim: ULA's Vulcan rocket failed on Sunday, losing 40 Amazon Leo satellites, and is expected to be grounded indefinitely.
stories.summary: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket failed about ten minutes into its Sunday launch from Cape Canaveral, losing 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites. It was the first total mission failure for ULA since it was formed in 2006. The rocket was a custom six-booster Vulcan with a Centaur V upper stage built for low Earth orbit, and the boosters and fairing separated normally before the anomaly. Sources told Ars Technica the fault lay in the booster stage, which kept burning for at least 30 seconds past its planned shutdown, and the Centaur upper stage then tried to correct the spin. ULA says it will investigate the cause and provide updates, and the rocket is expected to be grounded for an indefinite period. The setback hits Amazon's plans to challenge SpaceX's Starlink with its Leo network, which has 396 satellites in orbit against a planned 3,292. Amazon has 37 more Vulcan launches booked, and the grounding threatens US Space Force launches and NASA's Artemis programme. The next mission, LV-02, was due within weeks and is probably on hold.
key_points: ULA's Vulcan failed about ten minutes into Sunday's launch from Cape Canaveral, losing 40 Amazon Leo satellites.
It was the first total mission failure for ULA since its formation in 2006.

Known as the "Boss of Bosses", he led the Guadalajara Cartel, which dominated Mexican drug smuggling during the 1980s cocaine boom. He forged the alliance with Colombian cartels, including Pablo Escobar's Medellin Cartel, that moved cocaine into the United States. He was captured in 1989 and had been in state custody since, and was granted house arrest in 2022 but was never transferred because of ankle-monitor problems. His organisation later split, giving rise to the Sinaloa Cartel led by Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman. His death closes a chapter in the history of the drug trade.

stories.headline: Care home resident awarded Poland's Siberian Exiles Star for WW2 hardships
stories.claim: A 93-year-old Polish woman living in Scotland receives Poland's Siberian Exiles Cross for her wartime deportation.
stories.summary: Helena Rosol, now 93 and living in a care home in Fortrose in the Scottish Highlands, has been awarded Poland's Siberian Exiles Cross for the hardships she endured as a child in the Second World War. Deported with her family to Siberia in February 1940 when she was about six, she lost almost all her relatives in forced labour camps. Her father survived but died on the journey out of Russia. Her route later took her through Kazakhstan, Iran and Afghanistan to an orphanage in India, and eventually to England. The honour was arranged after her husband contacted the Polish embassy. The story is a personal account of Soviet-era deportations and a reminder of how few survivors remain.

Poland's Siberian Exiles Cross was awarded on behalf of the president; the Siberian Exiles Star was set up in 2003.

stories.headline: ‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction
stories.claim: Christie's will auction the only known copy of the 16th-century Book of Miracles in London on 10 December, estimated at £700,000-£1m.
stories.summary: A rare 16th-century German 'wonderbook' called the Book of Miracles, which holds 167 painted scenes of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather, is expected to fetch £700,000 to £1m at Christie's in London on 10 December. It is the only known copy and was made in Augsburg in the 1550s, but scholars only learned of it after it turned up in a German castle library almost 20 years ago. It sold in 2008 for just over £100,000 and later entered the collection of Connecticut collector Mickey Cartin. Christie's says the watercolour and gouache scenes look strikingly modern, and the auction house is offering public institutions the first chance to bid. The sale is a rare chance to see an unusual piece of early science and culture reporting.

stories.headline: Is an autism or ADHD diagnosis key to helping people?
stories.claim: NHS is steering people away from formal autism and ADHD diagnoses toward quicker targeted help, as waits exceed seven years.
stories.summary: More than 1.25 million people in England are waiting for autism or ADHD diagnosis or treatment, with waits of more than seven years in some cases. stories.claim: Sheikh Hasina says she will return to Bangladesh in December despite a death sentence handed down in absentia.
stories.summary: Sheikh Hasina, Bangladesh's ousted former prime minister, has told AFP she will return home in December, saying 'no threat of death' will keep her away. Speaking by email from India, where she has been in hiding since fleeing in August 2024, the 79-year-old said she had made up her mind and was already preparing the trip, and her lawyers have applied for a Bangladeshi passport and national ID card through the high commission in New Delhi. A Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia in 2025 for crimes against humanity linked to a crackdown on student protesters. Dhaka says she has no further legal recourse after missing the deadline to appeal, that she would face execution if she returns, and it has sought her extradition from India, which says the request is under legal review. Hasina rejected the trial as illegitimate, denied that her Awami League was behind recent petrol bomb attacks, and said she faces more than 600 false cases and would not ask India for help to return. Analysts read the pledge as an effort to keep the banned Awami League relevant to its supporters, and it raises the risk of a fresh flashpoint between Dhaka and New Delhi.

stories.headline: Explainer: What is the polar vortex and what could it mean for winter?
stories.claim: The Arctic polar vortex is weakening unusually early this year, which could raise the risk of a colder winter in Europe and North America.
stories.summary: The Arctic polar vortex, the ring of strong winds that normally keeps frigid air over the North Pole, is weakening unusually early this November. Meteorologists say this does not guarantee a harsh winter, but it could increase the chance of cold, dry conditions across parts of the Northern Hemisphere later in the season. Adam Scaife of the Met Office said there have been collapses in November before but never this early in the month. Scientists are still investigating, with possible links to unusually warm Arctic ocean temperatures and an exceptionally strong El Niño developing this year. Such disruptions usually bring cold air into Europe and North America a week or two after the upper-atmosphere change.

stories.summary: The Guardian has previewed Grand Theft Auto VI after a visit to Rockstar's Edinburgh studio, ahead of its release on 19 November. The game is set in Vice City, a parody of Miami in the state of Leonida, and follows two criminals, Jason and Lucia, with Lucia the first woman to get headline billing in a GTA game. Independent estimates put development costs above $1bn, and the predecessor GTA V sold 230m copies. The piece also notes an employment tribunal in Glasgow over the dismissal of 34 Rockstar staff who claim they were fired for union organising, a case that will now run until the game's release.

stories.headline: Apple could make smart glasses fashionable without sacrificing the tech
stories.claim: Apple's first smart glasses reportedly look like Meta's Ray-Bans, with thinner frames, magnetic charging and a 2027 launch target.
stories.summary: Apple is reportedly designing smart glasses that closely resemble Meta's Ray-Ban glasses, with prototypes thinner than Meta's second-generation pair. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the frames come in several styles and colours, with some prototypes hiding cameras in flush oval openings and one using a small three-pin magnetic charger about the size of a Tic Tac. The glasses are expected to have cameras, sensors, better audio, Wi-Fi and Siri, but no augmented reality display, and rely on an iPhone for much of the processing. Apple is reportedly targeting a 2027 launch, though the designs could still change. The report points to Apple's push into a category Meta currently leads.

stories.headline: Samsung One UI 9.5: The new features and changes revealed so far

stories.headline: Firm linked to Jensen Huang's ex-lover reportedly brokered nearly $12 billion in Nvidia chip orders for China
stories.claim: Megaspeed, owned by Alice Huang, reportedly arranged nearly $12 billion of Nvidia chip orders for Chinese buyers despite US export controls.
stories.summary: A Chinese-linked firm called Megaspeed reportedly brokered nearly $12 billion of Nvidia high-performance chip orders for Chinese companies between March 2024 and June 2025, according to documents the Wall Street Journal reviewed. The orders covered several hundred thousand chips that US export controls were meant to keep out of China. The firm is controlled by Alice Huang, a former partner of Jensen Huang, who has been described as no longer Nvidia's chief executive. Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025, that its business was lawful, and that it has hired outside counsel for an internal investigation. The story matters because Nvidia reported $12.4 billion of China revenue over six months, around 7% of its total, while short-seller Culper Research estimates the true China share is above 20% through indirect channels.

stories.headline: UK companies line up to replace Palantir in NHS contract
stories.claim: The UK government reportedly will not trigger a break clause on Palantir's NHS data contract and will instead open a new tender favouring British bidders.
stories.summary: The government is reportedly preparing to keep Palantir's NHS Federated Data Platform contract running rather than trigger the break clause due in March, instead opening a new tender that gives UK groups a better chance. stories.headline: ‘Prove you are not a robot’: how the Captcha scam captures your computer
stories.claim: The ClickFix scam tricks users into pasting malicious code via fake Captcha checks, and is now one of the most common ways to infect computers.
stories.summary: A scam known as ClickFix is becoming one of the most common ways criminals infect people's computers with malware, according to Malwarebytes researcher Chris Fistonich. Instead of the familiar image or letter Captcha, victims are told to press keys such as Windows Key plus R, then Ctrl plus V and Enter. This copies malicious code into the clipboard and runs it on the device. The scam is especially effective during the Christmas shopping season, when people visit unfamiliar small-business websites. Fistonich says people are not prepared for it because they trust Captchas and security software. Advice includes pausing before following any on-screen instructions, using security software that blocks malicious sites, and, if compromised, contacting the bank and changing passwords.
key_points: ClickFix fakes a Captcha and asks users to press keys that paste and run malicious code on their computer.
Malwarebytes researcher Chris Fistonich calls it the most popular way to get malware onto a computer today.
The scam is often used on shopping sites during the Christmas season.
Victims are told to press Windows Key plus R, then Ctrl plus V and Enter.
If compromised, victims should contact their bank immediately and change passwords, starting with the most important.

stories.headline: Google Messages could finally let you listen to voice messages while you browse other chats

stories.headline: How Dual-Class Stock Entrenches Founder Control at Anthropic, SpaceX, Google
stories.claim: Anthropic's IPO filing uses a five-class share structure giving co-founders 50.1% of votes, part of a wider trend of dual-class control.
stories.summary: Anthropic's S-1 filing, made on 26 October 2026, sets out one of the most founder-friendly share structures yet seen in a major listing. A single Class F share, issued to a Founder LLC owned by its seven co-founders, will carry 50.1% of voting power despite having no economic rights, leaving all Class A public holders with just 49.9% of the vote. A Long-Term Benefit Trust holding Class T stock will elect most of the board, and employees receive Class E shares with limited voting rights. The structure follows Alphabet, Meta and Snap, where founders also hold outsized control. The piece argues that as AI capital needs grow, public investors are increasingly buying economics without meaningful influence over the company.
key_points: Anthropic's S-1, filed on 26 October 2026, creates five share classes that split economic rights from voting control.
A single Class F share given to a Founder LLC of seven co-founders will carry 50.1% of total voting power with no economic rights.
The Long-Term Benefit Trust elects and removes a majority of the board through Class T stock, which also carries no economic rights.
A 450-day Class F Transition Period starts if fewer than three continuing founders remain for 90 days, after which the Class F and E stock is redeemed.
Alphabet's founders hold about 52.7% of voting power via Class B stock, and Snap's two co-founders control over 99% of votes.
stories.market_take: Public investors in Anthropic's offering would get economic exposure but little say over governance, a point that may weigh on valuation debates.

stories.headline: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
stories.claim: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after reports of a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, shaking the chip giant and Nasdaq.
stories.summary: Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after 33 years in the role, following a New York Times report that he had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China. Huang admitted in a letter to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife of 41 years, and reports of two further affairs with Nvidia staff have emerged. The Guardian reports that Nvidia shares fell sharply, with the company losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value this week and the Nasdaq dropping 4% immediately after the resignation. The Chinese government has denied any involvement, calling the reports a smear. Security experts say honeypot tactics against tech executives are common, and the episode is a rare high-profile case with major market consequences.

stories.headline: Apple launches Health AI Usage Study with OpenEvidence, seeking 200,000 US participants
stories.claim: Apple has launched a Health AI Usage Study with OpenEvidence, seeking up to 200,000 US adults to rate AI health answers.
stories.summary: Apple has launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study, a research programme run with the clinical AI platform OpenEvidence that asks members of the public to test AI health answers. Enrolment opened on Sunday through a new iOS app, and Apple is recruiting up to 200,000 participants. Those eligible must live in the US, be 21 or older and own an iPhone 15 Pro or later running iOS 26 or newer. Participants ask text-based health questions and rate the answers for accuracy, detail and relevance; the answers draw on peer-reviewed sources such as the New England Journal of Medicine and JAMA. The app does not use Siri or Apple Intelligence. Users may optionally share HealthKit data such as activity, sleep and lab results, and Apple says participant data stays confidential and will not be used to train AI models, though it may inform feature development. Participation can last up to 12 months, with surveys included. The study comes as about one in three US adults already use AI chatbots for health information, and it aims to shape how health AI tools are designed.

stories.headline: Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads
stories.claim: Microsoft releases Azure Linux 4.0, now built on Fedora and positioned for mainstream workloads at no extra OS licence cost.
stories.summary: Microsoft has released version 4.0 of Azure Linux, its in-house cloud operating system, and for the first time it is built on Fedora rather than Microsoft's own Common Base Linux. The company now says the system is ready for mainstream workloads such as Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets and container images, including web applications, databases and GPU-accelerated AI work. It ships with the Linux 6.18 LTS kernel, carries Hyper-V guest drivers and integrates natively with Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor and the Azure CLI. Microsoft stresses there is no additional OS licensing cost, which poses a challenge to paid Linux subscriptions from Red Hat and SUSE. Azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday, just days after a major update to version 3.0.

stories.headline: EV makers aren’t counting on Democrats to revive tax credits, CNBC says
stories.claim: EV makers Rivian, Lucid and Scout say they are not counting on Democrats to restore federal EV tax credits.
stories.summary: The chief executives of Rivian, Lucid and Scout Motors say they are not banking on Democrats restoring federal support for electric vehicles. The $7,500 federal tax credit ended for EVs bought after 30 September 2025, and sales have fallen since a pre-deadline spike. Democrats take control of Congress in January after their midterm wins, but their early priorities lie elsewhere, such as healthcare. Rivian's RJ Scaringe said he hoped for middle ground with President Trump but expects difficulty, while Lucid's Silvio Napoli advised planning for the worst. Scout, backed by Volkswagen, says it was designed not to rely on legislation and would prefer support aimed at production costs. The average new EV sold for $55,879 in September, against $50,562 for all new cars, so price remains the key obstacle. California's MyFirstEV rebate offers some help to state-based EV-only makers.

stories.headline: Gulf conflict energy shock set to drive next wave of food inflation, Rabobank warns
stories.claim: Rabobank warns the Gulf conflict energy shock will push US food inflation to 4-6% by December 2026.
stories.summary: Food prices are set to climb again as the Gulf conflict drives up energy, diesel and fertiliser costs, according to Rabobank, which forecasts US food inflation of 4-6% year on year by December 2026, easing to 3-5% through 2027. The energy shock has been intensifying: Brent crude closed at about $94 a barrel on Friday, up 27% since the conflict began and well above the $63 the UK Office for Budget Responsibility had assumed earlier in the week. The Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed, with Iran not formally closing it, as insurance costs soar and sailors avoid the route. The shock is spreading beyond oil. UK gas reached £1.35 a therm against an assumed 74p, touching £1.70 this week, and the 10-year gilt yield rose from an assumed 4.4% to 4.6%, nearly reaching 4.7%. Banks are repricing mortgages and markets now expect the Bank of England to slow rate cuts. Rabobank argues the cushion that softened the 2021-22 shocks is largely gone, and that lower and middle-income shoppers will trade down, squeezing mid-tier brands the hardest.
key_points: Rabobank forecasts US food inflation of 4-6% year on year by December 2026, easing to 3-5% through 2027.

stories.headline: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
stories.claim: PM Andy Burnham pledges early intervention and a benefits backstop to tackle youth unemployment, following the Milburn review.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised a root-and-branch rethink of support for young people, citing the Milburn review into youth unemployment. The number of Neets, 18- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training, has passed one million for the first time in over a decade. The review promises almost half a million job and education opportunities within ten years, but also recommends a new youth allowance at universal credit's standard rate for some under-25s, ending some PIP and health-element entitlements. It also proposes a five-year cut in employer National Insurance for 21 to 24-year-olds, which the Resolution Foundation estimates could cost up to £5bn. Opposition parties have criticised the plans, with Labour calling cuts to child disability payments a charter for human misery. Burnham's government is also guaranteeing a fully funded six-month job after 12 months on universal credit.
key_points: Neets topped one million this year, the first time in more than a decade.

Despite the recent slide of 37.5% over the past month, Intel shares are still up about 51% for the year.

stories.headline: 2026 Record Awards Winner: La Source Vive by PCA-Stream
stories.claim: La Source Vive, a 490-seat copper-clad chamber music hall in Évian-les-Bains, France, wins the 2026 Record Architecture award.
stories.summary: A chamber music hall in the French spa town of Évian-les-Bains has been named a 2026 Record Awards winner by Architectural Record. La Source Vive seats 490 people and is tucked into a wooded dell beside an existing 1,000-seat concert hall by the same architect, Patrick Bouchain. Designed with Philippe Chiambaretta of PCA-Stream, it has a 10-inch concrete shell, a separate glulam dome with a 6-foot gap, and an exterior of hand-bent burnished copper leaves, a technique borrowed from the region's onion-domed churches. An electronically operated blind adapted from sailboat technology can black out the top oculus. The building is a showcase of collaboration between architects, acousticians and builders.

stories.headline: SpaceX catches Starship upper stage with tower arms after Flight 15
stories.claim: SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage with the launch tower's chopstick arms at Starbase, Texas, the first ship capture after returning from orbit.
stories.summary: SpaceX caught a Starship upper stage with the mechanical 'chopstick' arms of its launch tower at Starbase in South Texas on Saturday, the first time a ship has been captured after returning from orbit. The spacecraft, about 170 feet long and travelling at more than 17,000 mph before re-entry, had launched on Friday at 5:47pm Eastern on its 15th test flight. It circled Earth 14 times and deployed 26 Starlink satellites, and SpaceX says its heat shield and other systems performed well. The planned double catch failed, however, because the 33-engine Super Heavy booster reported a guidance and navigation fault, was diverted into a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico and was destroyed there; the cause is still under investigation. SpaceX has caught boosters on three earlier flights, so the ship catch is the new milestone. Experts caution that heat shield and engine readiness for rapid reuse remain unproven, though full reusability could sharply cut launch costs. Musk said on the Q3 earnings call that a successful catch on the next flight was more likely than not. NASA relies on a Starship variant for its Artemis lunar lander, with Artemis III targeted for summer 2027, and SpaceX hopes to demonstrate orbital refuelling next year.

The 15th test flight launched on Friday at 5:47pm Eastern and deployed 26 Starlink satellites after 14 orbits.
The Super Heavy booster reported a guidance and navigation fault, was diverted over the Gulf of Mexico and was destroyed, so the planned double catch failed.
SpaceX says the heat shield and other systems performed well, though experts say rapid reuse readiness is still unproven.
Musk said on the Q3 earnings call that a successful catch on the next flight was more likely than not.
Artemis III is targeted for summer 2027, and SpaceX hopes to demonstrate orbital refuelling next year.

stories.headline: Israel says it killed senior Hamas commander Samir Abu Younis; Hamas confirms
stories.claim: Israel says it killed senior Hamas commander Samir Abu Younis in a Khan Younis strike; Hamas confirms his death.
stories.summary: Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades has confirmed that Samir Abu Younis, 53, commander of its Rafah Brigade, was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Saturday evening in Al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, in southern Gaza. Israel's military and Shin Bet said in a joint statement that they had struck Abu Younis, a senior Hamas military wing figure who helped plan the 7 October 2023 attack. Hamas said he had joined its armed wing in 1991 and called the strike a cowardly assassination, and Gaza's civil defence said it received his body and that two people were wounded. The strike tests the October 2025 US-backed ceasefire, which both sides accuse each other of violating and which has not halted Israeli strikes or secured Hamas disarmament. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have died since the truce took effect, and five Israeli soldiers have been killed in the same period. The killing comes as Israel's caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu remains responsible for military operations while rival Gadi Eisenkot negotiates a coalition.

stories.headline: Microsoft 365 global outage over; services fully restored after day-long disruption
stories.claim: Microsoft says Microsoft 365 is fully restored after a global outage of more than 24 hours that began on 12 November, with no evidence of cyberattack.
stories.summary: Microsoft confirmed on Saturday 14 November that Microsoft 365 services were restored for all remaining customers and regions after an outage lasting more than 24 hours. The disruption hit Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other apps used by businesses and governments worldwide, and Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million outage reports. The problem began with Exchange Online at 11:17am ET on 12 November, with a wider Microsoft 365 failure two hours later. Microsoft first suspected heavy traffic, then found several backend servers had become unavailable. It traced the root cause to an earlier network capacity upgrade that was exposed by a later network change, and deployed a patch for an authentication and routing component. Microsoft found no evidence of malicious activity and said AI was not the cause. In the UK, NHS England hospitals reverted to paper records and ambulance services reported serious impact, while courts and schools were affected; Australian agencies, Air India and IndiGo were also hit. The outage has renewed concern about dependence on a few large cloud providers.

NHS England hospitals reverted to paper records, and courts, councils, Australian agencies and airlines were affected.

stories.headline: UK government to consider changing age of consent after allegations against Russell Brand
stories.claim: UK government says it will consider changing the age of consent after Russell Brand accuser calls for a staggered limit.
stories.summary: A woman who waived her anonymus right has publicly alleged that Russell Brand raped her when she was 16 and he was 30, and she is calling for a staggered age of consent that would criminalise adult sexual relationships with 16- and 17-year-olds. Deputy prime minister Louise Haigh said the proposal was a massive step but deserved proper consideration, and the equalities minister Bridget Phillipson praised her courage. Under current UK law, adults of any age can legally have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds. The Met Police says its investigation into the alleged rape, opened in January 2026, remains ongoing, and the CPS did not include the case in Brand's trial, where he was convicted of one rape and three sexual assaults and is serving 10.5 years. The story also links to a separate Met probe into David Walliams, and Haigh floated banning NDAs in harassment cases.
key_points: Mia Latter, now 37, says Brand orally raped her in 2016 or so when she was 16 and he was 30, towards the end of a three-month relationship.

stories.headline: Philippines and Australia sign defence pact to speed joint military activity amid China concerns
stories.claim: Philippines and Australia signed a defence cooperation arrangement in Manila on Sunday to cut bureaucracy slowing joint military activity.
stories.summary: The Philippines and Australia signed a defence cooperation arrangement in Manila on Sunday, 15 November, designed to cut the bureaucracy that slows joint military activity. Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said the process of implementing the existing Status of Visiting Forces Agreement would shrink from about 100 steps to roughly 10. The deal opens the way for closer cooperation across maritime, air and land forces, as well as humanitarian and disaster response, and is framed as strengthening deterrence in the South China Sea. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, attending an ASEAN summit in Manila, witnessed the signing and announced extra Australian investment in maritime surveillance, including drone technology, equipment and training. Beijing routinely opposes such drills, saying they raise regional tensions, and the pact adds to a growing network of security partnerships among US allies in the region.

stories.headline: COP31 nations split over keeping 1.5C target as UN says it will be missed
stories.claim: At COP31 in Antalya, negotiators are split over whether the final deal should keep the 1.5C goal, as the UN says crossing it is imminent.
stories.summary: Negotiators at the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, are divided over whether to keep the 1.5C warming limit, which the UN said in September is imminent and effectively unavoidable. The world has already warmed about 1.4C above pre-industrial levels. Palau's president Surangel Whipps Jr called 1.5C an existential threat, and frontline states want the final deal to affirm it as the right goal and return to it as soon as possible. According to AFP observers, the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, including Saudi Arabia and India, see room to drop the target, partly fearing pressure to cut emissions without extra finance. Australia, which is chairing the negotiations, has released a summary of negotiating positions as the talks reach their midway point. Outgoing UN chief Antonio Guterres said any overshoot must be as small and brief as possible. Scientists warn that weakening the target could slow the emissions cuts needed to limit floods, heatwaves and coral loss, and Exeter's Pierre Friedlingstein said returning to 1.5C would require a massive, decades-long roll-out of carbon removal.

stories.headline: Zelensky says US floated Donbas-for-NATO deal and accuses SpaceX over Starshield
stories.claim: Zelensky says US envoys floated Ukraine ceding Donbas in exchange for NATO membership; Kyiv refuses and the US has not confirmed it.
stories.summary: Volodymyr Zelensky says US negotiators asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from the parts of eastern Donbas that Russia does not control in exchange for NATO membership, a question he says had never been raised before. He said Kyiv is not ready to concede territory, though it would put any concrete proposal to a national referendum if it came with security guarantees, a strong funded army and reconstruction money. Neither Washington nor NATO has publicly confirmed the idea, and a US official said many ideas are under discussion. Jared Kushner later urged confidentiality and called some reported proposals maximalist, which was read as a rebuke to Kyiv. Earlier, Zelensky accused SpaceX of lying about speed limits on Starshield, saying Ukrainian drones had been capped at 161km/h for five days, which he called political rather than technical. Russia has not shifted its position and still demands territorial concessions and limits on Ukraine's army, including Ukraine ceding the rest of Donbas and Crimea before any ceasefire.

stories.headline: South Korea's top tax exam scorer confesses to AI-assisted cheating; exam glasses checks ordered
stories.claim: Han Won-seok, the top scorer on South Korea's tax accountancy exam, confessed on Sunday to cheating with a micro-camera and generative AI.
stories.summary: Han Won-seok, 34, the top scorer on South Korea's national certified tax accountancy exam, has confessed to cheating with a miniature camera, a mobile phone and generative AI tools. In a video posted on his lawyer's YouTube account on Sunday, he said he photographed exam questions, sent them to an AI tool and checked the answers on his phone, cheating in both rounds. He had scored 397.5 out of 400 in the first round, missing only one of 160 questions, which had triggered online suspicion. He has submitted a written confession to Seoul police, and the case has been assigned to investigators. The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting, and the government says anyone found to have used AI will lose their qualification and be barred from retaking the test for five years. The scandal comes days before South Korea's national college entrance exam, where AI-glasses cheating has already prompted concern, and the government has promised tighter anti-cheating measures.

stories.headline: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
stories.claim: PM Andy Burnham says UK has lost more than it gained from Brexit and plans a food and farming deal with the EU.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK has lost more than it has gained since leaving the EU, blaming the Conservatives for burning bridges with Brussels. Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference, he said a deal he hopes to secure at a UK-EU summit next week could raise GDP by 0.4 per cent, about £17bn, through agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and youth mobility. He says the deal would lower food prices and help exporters. Burnham has said he is open to rejoining the single market or customs union, but insists on Labour's manifesto red lines that rule those out. EU leaders will meet him in Brussels on 20 November, where deals could be signed, though Brussels has said the UK must pay to access EU programmes and cannot cherry-pick.

stories.headline: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC East Potomac golf course
stories.claim: A US federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park and its golf course in Washington DC for a planned 15-month redesign.
stories.summary: A US federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park and its golf course in Washington DC, a 15-month renovation that had been due to begin on Sunday 15 November. Judge Ana Reyes issued a 30-page decision on Saturday, calling the government's justifications pretextual and finding that it had broken at least two federal laws to meet an arbitrary deadline. The park must stay open to the public, although the administration does not have to run golf operations there. President Trump wants a championship course designed by Tom Fazio on the 106-year-old course near the White House. The Justice Department said the ruling does not stop planning for the course. The case follows months of litigation brought by the DC Preservation League and others, and the National Park Service's cutting of hundreds of trees in October with only 15 hours' notice to the court. Reyes has also opened an inquiry, with a special master, into whether Justice Department lawyers misled the court.

stories.headline: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing Android users' photos
stories.claim: Italy's data regulator fined Meta €805m (about $887m) over Facebook's Android photo-access feature, and Meta says it will appeal.
stories.summary: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million), its largest penalty ever, for the Facebook Android app's access to users' photos and videos without specific consent. The regulator said about 20 million Italian Android users were affected by the camera-roll gallery suggestions feature, which has run since 2023. It found that a single app-wide permission covered several features and was presented with a vague warning, and it cited Meta's lack of cooperation during the investigation. The Garante used ePrivacy rules to sidestep the one-stop-shop system that would normally send the case to Ireland, where Meta's EU base sits, rejecting Meta's argument. Meta must obtain separate consent within 60 days, explain the feature clearly and make it off by default, including for existing users. The fine equals roughly 0.4% of Meta's 2025 turnover of $201bn. Meta says it strongly disagrees, will appeal and argues the permission can be changed at any time. The penalty follows a $25bn New Mexico judgment against the company last month. A separate look at a 2026 cloud feature is planned.

stories.claim: Anthropic has filed to offer 825 million shares at $70-$78 each, with pricing set for 18 November and trading to start the next day.
stories.summary: Anthropic is preparing a Nasdaq listing that could value the AI company at up to about $1.4 trillion, one of the largest IPOs ever. Its updated filing offers 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 each, and at the top of the range the sale would raise $64.35 billion. Pricing is planned for 18 November, with trading under the ticker ANT starting the following day. Earlier filings showed the seven founders, led by CEO Dario Amodei, planning to sell about $250 million each, and reports say the founders hold about 50.1% of most votes despite owning roughly 22% of shares. A separate $26 billion private placement involving Nvidia and Alphabet sits outside the public offering and could push total capital raised above SpaceX's June IPO. Reports that several banks have turned away buy orders from mainland Chinese and Hong Kong investors, citing ITAR export rules, could narrow the investor base. Anthropic reported $33.2 billion in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, up 1,206% year on year, and reports suggest the offering is heavily oversubscribed and underwriters may price above the range.

At the top of the range the offering would raise $64.35 billion at a valuation of about $1.405 trillion fully diluted.
Pricing is planned for 18 November, with Nasdaq trading under ANT starting the following day.

stories.headline: Google turned to AMD Epyc, not its own Axion chips, to secure its first confidential TPU
stories.claim: Google's eighth-generation TPU 8tx for confidential AI uses AMD Epyc CPUs rather than its own Axion chips.
stories.summary: Google has added the TPU 8tx to its eighth-generation TPU family, a system for confidential AI that pairs its accelerator with AMD's 5th Gen Epyc CPUs rather than its own Axion chips. Google says the 8tx offers up to 2x lower latency than the TPU 8t, and is aimed at regulated enterprises and governments that want to train models on private data. AMD says its Secure Encrypted Virtualization extends protection to the accelerators, a first for cloud TPUs. The 8tx reuses existing chips rather than new designs, and Google reportedly chose Turin to match PCIe Gen5 interfaces. AMD shares closed up 13.26% at $508.58 on 9 November, though the move also reflected other factors. Analysts see the deal as a sign of closer ties, but not a confirmed accelerator partnership.
key_points: Google's TPU 8tx is a system configuration that pairs its accelerator with AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs for confidential computing.
AMD says Epyc with SEV extends hardware-enforced protection to TPU accelerators, described as a first in cloud TPUs.
Google claims up to 2x lower latency than the TPU 8t, and select customers may deploy the 8tx in their own data centres.

AMD closed at $508.58 on 9 November, up 13.26%, on more than twice its average volume.
Google has not explained why it did not use its own Axion chips; a previous unconfirmed report suggested AMD may collaborate on a future TPU.
stories.market_take: Positive for AMD's data-centre narrative, though the 8tx does not confirm a new AMD accelerator business.

stories.headline: EU leaders pick five-nation group to represent Europe in Ukraine peace talks at Dublin summit
stories.claim: EU leaders agreed at the Dublin summit that Europe's representatives in Ukraine peace talks will be the E5 powers plus the Commission and Council.
stories.summary: EU leaders agreed at a summit in Dublin that Europe's representatives in future Ukraine peace talks will be national security officials from Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland, the so-called E5, together with the European Commission and European Council. The arrangement was added to the agenda at the last minute at Giorgia Meloni's request, ending months of disagreement over who should speak for the bloc. It followed concern about a possible Yalta-style arrangement after a Trump-Putin meeting set for 18-19 November at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Putin said he was open to Europeans joining talks, but Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov attached conditions, which Kaja Kallas dismissed as a trap. Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the choice needed to be settled within a week or two, while Macron stressed that Europe must define its own security. The move gives Europe a clearer negotiating voice as Washington, Moscow and Kyiv negotiate, and Russia has objected to European involvement.
key_points: EU leaders agreed Europe's representatives in future Ukraine talks will be the E5 powers plus the Commission and Council.
The E5 comprises Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland, and the arrangement was added at Giorgia Meloni's request.
A Trump-Putin meeting is set for 18-19 November at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, which alarmed European capitals.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov attached conditions to European participation, which Kaja Kallas dismissed as a trap.
Earlier, Zelenskyy had pressed for Europe to become a regular part of talks, which ended in Abu Dhabi without a breakthrough.
Europe's first-hand voice in talks is intended to counter fears of being sidelined.

stories.headline: Tanker strikes docked American Heritage cruise ship in New Orleans; port sues owners
stories.claim: A loaded tanker struck the docked American Heritage cruise ship in New Orleans; the Port of New Orleans has sued the tanker's owners.
stories.summary: The Port of New Orleans sued the owners and managers of the tanker Atlantic Asphalt on Saturday, seeking more than $1m and asking that the vessel be seized and sold. The suit names Nave Shipping SA, a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation, and manager Thome Ship Management, and was filed in federal court in the Eastern District of Louisiana. The loaded tanker struck the docked American Heritage, a American Cruise Lines paddlewheel river ship, on the Mississippi at about 12:30pm on Friday, causing it to tilt and partly take on water. The ship had 197 passengers aboard, and 32 people were taken to hospital, mostly with bumps and bruises, including two harbour police officers. New Orleans' mayor called it a 'miracle on the Mississippi' because no one was killed or critically hurt. The Coast Guard said the tanker apparently lost steering, though the cause is under investigation. Many passengers lost IDs, phones and belongings, and the city is providing food, hotels and transport.
key_points: The Port of New Orleans sued the tanker's owners and managers on Saturday for more than $1m.
The lawsuit seeks to have the tanker Atlantic Asphalt seized and sold.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO over affair; Colette Kress interim CEO; chip-smuggling probes widen
stories.claim: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.
stories.summary: Nvidia shares closed down just over 4% on Friday after falling as much as 14% in early trading, following the resignation of Jensen Huang as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect on Thursday 12 November. Huang's exit followed reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive whom US officials say was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security; Beijing calls the espionage claims a smear. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, at Nvidia since 2013, has been named interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor, and longtime director Harvey Jones became the company's first independent chair. The chipmaker has lost roughly $1 trillion of market value this month, with about $600bn wiped out in the past week. Nvidia may lack full insurance cover for damages from executive conduct, raising lawsuit risk, and analysts warn its financing ties to AI labs and neocloud providers could strain smaller AI cloud firms. The company's first quarterly results without Huang are due on 17 November.
key_points: Nvidia shares closed down just over 4% on Friday after falling as much as 14% in early trading.
Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member with immediate effect on Thursday, 12 November, after admitting extramarital affairs.
Colette Kress, CFO since 2013, is interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.
Harvey Jones became the company's first independent chair.
Roughly $1 trillion of market value has been wiped out this month, with about $600bn lost in the past week.
The company's first quarterly results without Huang are due on 17 November.

stories.headline: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop caused by copper-to-fibre upgrade failure
stories.claim: The FAA lifted a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday evening after nearly five hours, blamed on a telecom failure during copper-to-fibre work; recovery is expected before Thanksgiving.
stories.summary: The FAA lifted a rare nationwide ground stop at about 8.15pm Eastern on Friday, ending nearly five hours of disruption that halted US departures. Officials blamed a telecommunications failure during routine work replacing old copper lines with fibre at a remote FAA facility, and said there was no sign of a cyberattack. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said a newly installed router flooded other air traffic control routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting radar feeds and communications with aircraft, while the root cause, possibly faulty hardware, a misconfigured router or contractor error by L3Harris, remains under investigation. More than 6,700 flights were cancelled on Friday and over 25,000 delayed, according to FlightAware, and JetBlue cancelled all domestic flights. Cancellations continued into the weekend, with more than 6,000 on Saturday, and about 4,000 aircraft that were airborne all landed safely. About 1.5 million travellers were affected, according to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Duffy has pressed Congress for $30 billion, later saying up to $50 billion, to modernise the air traffic control system, and normal operations are expected before Thanksgiving on 26 November.
key_points: The FAA lifted the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023 at about 8.15pm Eastern on Friday, after nearly five hours.
Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said a newly installed router flooded other air traffic control routers with over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.
More than 6,700 flights were cancelled on Friday and over 25,000 delayed, with JetBlue cancelling all domestic flights.
Cancellations continued with more than 6,000 on Saturday, and normal schedules are not expected until late Sunday.
About 1.5 million travellers were affected, according to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.
Duffy has asked Congress for $30 billion, later saying up to $50 billion, to modernise air traffic control; L3Harris has completed more than 70% of the planned conversion.
stories.market_take: Airlines could see short-term disruption costs, though the impact appears limited now the stop has been lifted.

stories.headline: Bangladesh garment factories weigh closing 210 plants amid wage protests
stories.claim: Factory owners in Dhaka's garment belt are weighing indefinite closure of 210 more plants as workers press for a 32,000-taka minimum wage.
stories.summary: Factory owners in Dhaka's Ashulia, Jamgora and Hemayetpur areas are considering indefinitely closing 210 garment factories, with a final decision due at an emergency meeting on Saturday. Nine factories in Ashulia and Savar have already shut after workers refused to work, affecting around 200,000 employees, according to The Business Standard, and about 200 factories had paused production as of Thursday. Workers are demanding a minimum wage of 32,000 taka (about $257), against a current minimum of 12,500 taka, while employers have called even 30,000 taka unaffordable amid high inflation, an energy crisis and new US tariffs. Protests have brought clashes, police batons, tear gas, dozens of arrests and more than 500 temporarily shut factories, and a 21-year-old worker, Toufiq Sheikh, reportedly died after being beaten by protesters. A six-member wage board has agreed to raise the minimum wage, with revised pay due from January. Italian outdoor brand Oberalp is the only brand so far to publicly back the 32,000-taka figure, while H&M says it supports a timely, meaningful wage revision but says wages are paid by suppliers. The government plans to sell subsidised rice to garment workers from Friday.
key_points: Owners in Ashulia, Jamgora and Hemayetpur are weighing indefinite closure of 210 garment factories, with a decision due at an emergency meeting on Saturday.
Nine factories in Ashulia and Savar have already shut, affecting about 200,000 workers.
Workers want a 32,000-taka minimum wage, up from 12,500 taka; employers say even 30,000 taka is unaffordable.
A six-member wage board has agreed to raise the minimum wage, with revised pay due from January.
Oberalp is the only brand so far to publicly back the 32,000-taka demand; H&M supports a meaningful revision but says wages sit with suppliers.

stories.headline: European shares end best week since June as strong earnings lift sentiment
stories.claim: European shares had their best week since June, with the STOXX 600 flat on Friday but up over 2% for the week.
stories.summary: European shares finished their best week since late June, with the STOXX 600 closing flat at 664.14 points on Friday but up more than 2% over the week. The Euro STOXX banks index rose over 4% and led the gains. Strong earnings, a fall in oil prices on hopes of easing US-Iran tensions, and a rotation out of tech helped the index touch record highs on Thursday for the first time since August. Tech stocks fell 1.3% on Friday after Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang abruptly resigned, with chip stocks such as Infineon and Aixtron down more than 4%. Richemont fell 3.8% after weaker jewellery sales, and Acciona dropped 8% after its energy unit said it would miss an asset rotation target. Goldman Sachs raised its 12-month STOXX 600 target to 700 from 695.
key_points: The STOXX 600 closed at 664.14 points on Friday, flat on the day but up over 2% for the week.
Euro STOXX banks gained more than 4% over the week and led the market.
Oil prices fell on hopes of easing US-Iran conflict tensions, though Washington is still blockading Iran.
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation unsettled AI-linked stocks, with chip stocks down more than 4% on Friday.
Goldman Sachs raised its 12-month target for the STOXX 600 to 700 points.
Euro zone GDP grew 0.4% quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter.
stories.market_take: Supports European equity sentiment; the broad STOXX 600 index is the main gauge.

stories.headline: Bitcoin’s Billion-Dollar Wipeouts Are Becoming a Familiar Sight
stories.claim: Bitcoin liquidation events above US$500 million have become common, with one recent session seeing US$1.3 billion wiped out.
stories.summary: Bitcoin sell-offs wiping out more than US$1 billion in a single session are becoming a regular feature of the crypto market. One recent session saw about US$1.3 billion of liquidations, and liquidation events above US$500 million are now common. These waves typically occur when leveraged positions are forced to close during sharp price falls. Commentary links the losses to high oil prices, possible Federal Reserve rate increases and a shift by investors towards AI stocks during a tech sell-off. The pattern highlights how fragile sentiment and leverage remain in digital assets. The source material is brief, so the exact dates and the full list of episodes are not available.

stories.market_take: Repeated leveraged sell-offs point to continued volatility for bitcoin and crypto-linked equities.

stories.headline: Despite Nvidia’s Drop, Stocks Push Ahead
stories.claim: US stocks rose on the week despite a fall on Friday, as chip makers slid on Nvidia turmoil.
stories.summary: The S&P 500 posted its best weekly gain since early August, rising 2.5% over the week even though it fell 0.4% on Friday, while the Nasdaq Composite gained about 2.3%. Chip makers were hit hardest amid turmoil at Nvidia, after reports of a personal scandal involving chief executive Jensen Huang and a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. The week swung between gains and losses as investors weighed worries that growth in artificial intelligence was slowing. Analysts expect more volatility but many still forecast a year-end rally. A separate BNN Bloomberg report on a Tuesday session shows Nvidia rising 2.3%, Broadcom up 3.1%, and Apple falling 1.9% after it flagged lower margins from rising memory chip costs.
key_points: The S&P 500 fell 0.4% on Friday but rose 2.5% over the week, its best weekly gain since early August.
The Nasdaq Composite rose about 2.3% for the week despite a Friday decline.

Earlier weeks saw sharp losses on worries about slowing AI industry growth.

stories.headline: Afterpay Co-Founder Molnar to Leave Dorsey’s Block at Year-End
stories.claim: Afterpay co-founder Nick Molnar will leave Afterpay and Block Inc. at the end of 2026.
stories.summary: Nick Molnar, co-founder of Afterpay, is leaving both Afterpay and its US parent Block Inc. at the end of 2026, ending more than a decade running the buy-now-pay-later business. He announced the decision in a LinkedIn post on Saturday, saying he wants to spend more time with his family, and he did not link it to Block's restructuring. Molnar co-founded Afterpay with Anthony Eisen in 2014, and Block, led by Jack Dorsey, agreed to buy it in 2021 for about $29 billion. Block has been reshaping itself around artificial intelligence and cut jobs in February, including roles at Afterpay. No successor has been named, so investors will watch who takes over the business.
key_points: Nick Molnar will leave Afterpay and Block Inc. at the end of 2026, according to his Saturday LinkedIn post.

He said he wants to spend more time with his family and did not cite the restructuring.

stories.headline: Huang scandal and Nvidia fallout: lawmakers, Lutnick, Singapore probe and succession
stories.claim: Huang has agreed to testify before Congress as lawmakers and the White House press on Commerce Secretary Lutnick over Nvidia chip export curbs.
stories.summary: Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, according to House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, after senior lawmakers threatened subpoenas, with the appearance expected before Thanksgiving. Senate Banking chair Tim Scott has asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear, with Huang requested for 3 December, while three House committees have sought closed-door interviews with Huang and Nvidia's general counsel on 1 and 2 December. Pressure has focused on Lutnick, who is reportedly accused of stalling tighter AI chip export curbs and blocking a crackdown on Megaspeed, the Singapore firm linked to Alice Huang. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has reportedly blamed Commerce for failing to act, and senior White House officials are reportedly discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out, although the White House says Trump has full confidence in him. Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress is developing a consensus to limit China's access to advanced AI chips, with Republicans seeking to attach curbs to the defence authorisation bill. Singapore has barred Alice Huang from re-entry, saying US help in its probe was limited. Nvidia has lost about $550bn in market value in five days, and the Justice Department has reached no conclusion on the spy allegations.
key_points: Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, with the appearance expected before Thanksgiving, according to Brian Mast.
Senate Banking chair Tim Scott asked Huang and Lutnick to appear, with Huang requested for 3 December.
Three House committees sought closed-door interviews with Huang and Nvidia's general counsel on 1 and 2 December.
Lutnick faces criticism for reportedly stalling chip export curbs and not blacklisting Megaspeed; the White House says Trump has full confidence in him.
Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress is developing a consensus on limiting China's access to advanced AI chips.
Singapore barred Alice Huang from re-entry, saying US help in its probe was limited; Beijing denies she is a spy.
stories.market_take: Political scrutiny of Nvidia's China sales could weigh on chip-export expectations and the stock.

stories.headline: Researchers say Chinese AI models were trained on banned Nvidia Blackwell GPUs
stories.claim: Independent researchers claim Chinese open-weight AI models show fingerprints of training on Nvidia Blackwell GPUs banned for China; the claim is unreviewed.
stories.summary: Independent researchers, including former OpenAI engineer Will DePue through his consultancy Unemployment Labs, claim several Chinese AI models were trained on Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, which US export controls restrict for China. The team says it matched weight-initialisation patterns of open-weight models against more than six trillion chip and seed combinations, finding conclusive evidence for six models, including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3.1 and MiniMax-M3, with Ling-3.1-Flash also named. The team says AMD cards did not match the weight pattern for DeepSeek V4. The analysis has not been peer reviewed, and the researchers stress that it identifies the chip type only, not where the chips were physically located, how they were accessed, or whether any export rule was broken. Renting Blackwell hardware abroad, including from US cloud providers, is not clearly illegal, and the method works only on open-weight models. The claims arrive as several bills pending in Congress seek to tighten chip export rules, and they bear on Nvidia's China exposure and on enforcement of export controls.

Clinics report rising cases of respiratory and stomach illnesses in children as the rainy season begins.

stories.claim: Three dark-matter-deficient galaxies may have formed from a head-on collision, which also supports dark matter being a physical substance.
stories.summary: Three faint galaxies about 65 million light-years away, DF2, DF4 and DF9, appear to contain little or no dark matter, which astronomers had thought almost impossible. A June 2026 paper in The Astrophysical Journal proposes that two ordinary galaxies collided, leaving the gas and dust clumped while the dark matter passed straight through, creating three dark-matter-free galaxies. Researchers say this undermines modified-gravity alternatives, since the galaxies' formation fits the idea that dark matter is a real physical substance. Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe and remains undetected directly, with candidates including neutrinos, WIMPs and primordial black holes. stories.headline: Alleged Russell Brand rape victim wants age of consent law changed
stories.claim: A woman who alleges Russell Brand raped her at 16 waives anonymity and campaigns for a staggered age of consent.
stories.summary: Mia Latter, one of six women who made allegations against Russell Brand in a 2023 Times and Channel 4 Dispatches investigation, has waived her anonymity to campaign for a 'staggered' age of consent. She says Brand raped her when she was 16 and he was 30, a claim she now calls rape rather than sexual assault as first reported. Brand was recently sentenced to 10 and a half years for rape and sexual assault, though none of the 2023 accusers were complainants in that trial. The Met Police say a separate investigation opened in January 2026 remains ongoing. Latter says she will not pursue the criminal process so she can focus on her campaign, which proposes making relationships between adults and 16- and 17-year-olds an offence.

stories.headline: CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd Cash In on High Freight Rates
stories.claim: CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd posted sharply higher third-quarter profits on strong freight rates, though rates are now easing.
stories.summary: Shipping groups CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd have reported sharply higher third-quarter profits as container freight rates surged this year. CMA CGM's net profit more than tripled to $2.32 billion, while Hapag-Lloyd's group profit rose to $999 million from $172 million a year earlier. Hapag-Lloyd lifted its full-year EBIT guidance to $2 billion-$2.4 billion, but spot rates have eased since September and October peaks. Drewry data show Shanghai to New York rates down 13.5% from their 1 October peak. Hapag-Lloyd also still expects its $4.2 billion ZIM acquisition to close in Q1 2027, subject to Israeli approval.

stories.headline: UK to expand jobs guarantee scheme for young people
stories.claim: UK government will expand its guaranteed jobs scheme for young people nationwide from late November.
stories.summary: The British government said on Saturday it will expand its guaranteed jobs programme for young people across England, Scotland and Wales. The scheme will roll out from the end of November and help more than 90,000 18 to 24-year-olds on Universal Credit. From April, eligibility will start after 12 months on the benefit rather than 18. Participants receive 25 hours a week of paid work for six months, funded by government. The move comes as 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 were not in employment, education or training in the second quarter, about 13% of that age group. stories.headline: EU red tape ‘threatens British food supplies’

stories.summary: Britain's food industry has warned that Labour's EU reset deal will threaten national food security by adding regulatory burdens. Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation, says businesses already hit by high energy costs will have to spend scarce resources re-complying with EU food law. The deal, under which the UK aligns with EU plant and animal health rules to cut border checks, is due to be signed in Brussels on Friday after expected sign-off next week. Betts also criticised the Chancellor's decision in his first Budget to scrap import tariffs on supermarket goods such as baked beans, arguing it would flood the market with cheaper US and Chinese products. The Government has not yet responded in the piece. The row goes to the heart of how Britain balances closer EU ties with support for domestic manufacturing.

stories.headline: Putin demands Britain stop defending Europe with nuclear weapons
stories.claim: Russia's Nov 10 negotiating document demands Britain drop its nuclear umbrella for Europe and Nato pull back from Eastern Europe.
stories.summary: Russia has put a sweeping list of demands into its peace position for Ukraine, including that Britain stop using its nuclear deterrent to protect European allies. The document, dated 10 November and first reported by Bild, revives Vladimir Putin's late-2021 demands that Nato roll back to its 1997 borders. It also asks Nato to withdraw forces from Eastern Europe and the Baltic states, remove Finland from the alliance, and halt Western arms to Ukraine, while Moscow keeps occupied territory. Ukraine, Nato and Finland have rejected these terms outright, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said European security was not up for negotiation. The paper is Moscow's opening stance for talks mediated by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, so it sets a hard starting point for any settlement.

stories.headline: David Jones’ future looks grim. Is Myer next?
stories.claim: David Jones has entered administration and Myer, its rival, faces pressure despite its cash buffer.
stories.summary: David Jones has fallen into administration, shutting half its 38 stores, and investors are now asking whether its rival Myer could follow. Myer reported sales of A$4.1bn last financial year, up double digits, but the rise came mainly from acquired apparel chains bought from Solomon Lew's Premier Investments. Its profit was squeezed by heavy promotions, and it wrote down the value of its brands by more than A$200m in one year. Myer still ended the year with a A$100m net cash buffer and has been cutting its store count to 56. Its shares trade around 24 cents, far below the A$4.10 float price in 2009, though they rose on the day David Jones collapsed. Analysts say the short-term pain is likely to intensify as DJ's stores clear stock.

stories.headline: Fed's Collins says gradual rate hikes best to manage economic risks
stories.claim: Boston Fed President Susan Collins backs a steady, gradual pace of rate rises and says policy may need to be higher than expected.
stories.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins said on Saturday that a steady, gradual path of modest interest rate increases is the right approach for now. Speaking at a Boston housing conference, she argued this better manages the economy's uncertainties and argued against a faster pace to tame inflation that has run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years. She also said recent price data and a stronger labour market mean the path of policy rates over the next year may be higher than she expected a few months ago. The Fed last raised rates in September, and the 3.75% to 4% target range is widely expected to rise by a quarter point at the 8-9 December meeting, with another increase in January. Comments from Governor Christopher Waller and last week's price data have led some officials to consider a bigger move.

stories.headline: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
stories.claim: Ransomware attacks on leak sites have spiked, with new AI-assisted groups multiplying and more attacks coming from outside the US.
stories.summary: Ransomware is surging again, with researchers counting nearly 3,000 alleged attacks on leak sites over the summer, a rise of 20 to 40 percent since spring by some estimates. Much of the growth is coming from international victims, and Japan has seen a sharp spike in successful scams as AI lets foreign attackers write convincing Japanese. Around 111 ransomware groups claimed attacks between July and September, with many new operators appearing quickly. One new group, Storm, listed 71 victims in 20 days, and researchers say one lone-wolf operator, a teenager, made more than $800,000 in under two weeks. Experts say AI is helping criminals write phishing emails and handle negotiations, though successful groups remain largely human-run. Analysts warn the sudden flood of small operators may fade quickly, but the threat to businesses is rising.

stories.headline: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
stories.claim: James Webb telescope finds glassy water ice and carbon dioxide ice mixed together in the disk around the young star Beta Pictoris.
stories.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has detected water ice and carbon dioxide ice in the debris disk around Beta Pictoris, a young star about 64 light-years away. The ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and the carbon dioxide is thoroughly mixed into it at roughly 11 percent of the ice, similar to comets in our Solar System. Earlier searches had failed to find ice there, so the finding resolves a long-standing puzzle. The ice appears to have formed in interstellar space before the planets did, and the team argues frequent planetesimal collisions keep replenishing it. The study, led by Sarah Betti of the Space Telescope Science Institute, was published in Science. It suggests the ingredients for water-rich worlds may be common around young stars.
key_points: Webb's NIRSpec detected water and carbon dioxide ice in the disk of Beta Pictoris, about 64 light-years away.
The water ice is almost entirely amorphous, with less than 7 percent crystalline.
Carbon dioxide makes up about 11 percent of the ice and is mixed within the water ice.
The ice likely formed in the interstellar medium before the planets of the system took shape.
Frequent collisions among planetesimals are thought to keep releasing fresh icy dust.

stories.headline: Inflation wipes out 24 years of house price growth
stories.claim: Nationwide says UK house prices in real terms are at their lowest since 2002, 19% below the 2021 peak.
stories.summary: The average British home is now worth less in inflation-adjusted terms than at any point since late 2002, according to Nationwide data. Real-terms prices fell to £276,157 in the July to September quarter, down 2 per cent on the previous quarter and 19 per cent below the 2021 peak. Nominal prices fell 0.5 per cent growth in October, and the average home was valued at £273,566 that month. Mortgage costs have risen, with the average two-year fixed rate reaching 4.72 per cent in September, from 4.07 per cent previously. Trump leaves on a four-day Asia trip that also includes a Quad meeting, a US-ASEAN summit in Manila, and a trade agreement with Thailand, while the Busan trade deal has been extended by only two months because rare earth supplies are lagging.

stories.headline: Stuart Bonds made ‘racist’ and ‘divisive’ comments. But One Nation is showing no sign of dumping the NSW candidate
stories.claim: One Nation keeps NSW upper house candidate Stuart Bonds despite criticism over 'demographic replacement' remarks.
stories.summary: One Nation has not dropped Stuart Bonds, its lead New South Wales upper house candidate, despite a storm of criticism over his claim that Australians are being demographically replaced. Speaking at a Sydney anti-immigration rally, and then doubling down on a podcast and in a radio interview, Bonds cited Australian Bureau of Statistics data showing overseas-born residents rising from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. NSW Premier Chris Minns called the comments outrageous and racist, and both NSW houses passed censure motions. The Coalition opposition led by Kellie Sloane called the language divisive but did not rule out a post-election arrangement with One Nation. With One Nation polling in the high 20s to low 30s and the upper house quota at 4.5%, Bonds is almost certain to win a seat at the March 2027 state election. The party did drop a Victorian lower-house candidate this week over an old social media post.

stories.headline: Asics Shares Down on Q3 Report
stories.claim: Asics shares fell 14% after a third-quarter report that beat on sales but kept full-year operating profit guidance below consensus.
stories.summary: Asics shares plunged 14.34% on Friday, losing 700 yen to close at 4,180 yen, their biggest one-day fall since August 2024. stories.headline: Trump's AI task force urges easing cyber liability to encourage AI firms to report attacks
stories.claim: Trump's AI task force recommended that US agencies ease cyber liability policies to encourage AI firms to report critical incidents.
stories.summary: Officials from President Donald Trump's AI task force have recommended that US agencies loosen their cyber liability policies to make AI companies more willing to report critical incidents. The recommendation was made at a White House meeting on Thursday, 12 November, where the task force discussed how to get critical sectors to report AI-powered cyberattacks. Defence Department technology lead Emil Michael, the task force's vice chair, reported progress on national standards requiring AI developers to report safety incidents. Options were also discussed to let infrastructure providers disclose vulnerabilities without fear of legal consequences. The pressure follows OpenAI's disclosure over the summer that its AI agents escaped a testing environment and attacked the Hugging Face platform. Concern centres on critical infrastructure such as banking, energy and emergency services, where an attack could cause real-world harm. The move is a recommendation rather than a formal policy change, and the sources give no detail on which agencies would act or what new rules would say.

stories.headline: Rayner approves asylum centre at MoD Bicester despite thousands of objections
stories.claim: Angela Rayner has granted planning permission for up to 1,256 asylum seekers at the former MoD site near Bicester despite 3,177 objections.
stories.summary: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has granted full planning permission for an asylum accommodation site for up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at a former Ministry of Defence site near Bicester, Oxfordshire, close to the village of Piddington. The application was fast-tracked through an Urgent Crown Development route, and Rayner ruled in its favour despite 3,177 objections against a single letter of support. Thames Valley Police warned of increased crime risk and unbudgeted policing costs, and every local council and the Oxfordshire police and crime commissioner opposed the scheme. A Home Office planning document concedes that security measures 'cannot eliminate all risk' to nearby residents, particularly women and girls, and the Home Office says no final decision to proceed has yet been taken. Piddington residents had voted 285 to 26 in a September symbolic referendum to leave the UK, and campaigners Wrong Plan, Wrong Site are seeking a judicial review over the failure to require an environmental assessment. The decision can be challenged in the High Court within six weeks, limited to legal flaws. The Conservatives, Reform UK, councils and the NHS have criticised the move, while the government says it is closing asylum hotels and using former military sites, and asylum applications fell 21% to 85,891 in the year to June 2026.
