stories.headline: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet so AI agents can pay for purchases, US only at first
stories.claim: OpenAI has launched ChatGPT Wallet, letting its AI agents make purchases for users in the US, with card details hidden behind tokens.
stories.summary: OpenAI has launched ChatGPT Wallet, a payment feature that lets its AI agent buy goods on users' behalf, in a second attempt at AI shopping after scrapping its earlier Instant Checkout tool. At launch it works only in the US, through payments partner Dots, and requires a ChatGPT Pro subscription, an eligible US bank card and adult users. Each purchase shows the items, total and card and must be approved with Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Card numbers are replaced by transaction-specific tokens issued by American Express, Mastercard and Visa, so the agent and merchants never see the real card, and existing card rewards and dispute rights still apply. OpenAI takes no commission at the outset and says it will eventually allow fully hands-off purchases within set spending limits, categories and timeframes. The move puts OpenAI level with rivals such as Anthropic, Meta, xAI, Google and Perplexity, and OpenAI released a Commerce Partner Playbook to help merchants get past bot blocks.

stories.headline: Global oil supply returns to surplus for first time since start of Iran war, says IEA
stories.claim: IEA says global oil supply returned to surplus in October for the first time since the Iran war began.
stories.summary: Global oil supply ran about 2 million barrels a day ahead of demand in October, the first surplus since the US-Israeli war with Iran began, according to the International Energy Agency. Members will accelerate release of 71 million barrels of emergency stocks by end-February. The IEA also cut its 2026 demand forecast by 2.68 million barrels a day to 103.2 million. stories.summary: Italian e-tailer LuisaViaRoma is being sold to a group of Italian investors behind ATO SpA for 18.83 million euros, the same as the starting bid set by a Florence court. No rival bid was made, not even from Arav, the owner of John Richmond and Silvian Heach, which had said in October it was considering a bid. The deal ends more than a year of trouble for the retailer, which filed for a simplified composition procedure in March 2026. Completion is expected within weeks, and the business will be run by the current lessee LVR Srl under existing management.
key_points: ATO SpA's offer is worth 18.83 million euros: 4 million in cash plus 14.8 million in assumed liabilities.
A possible 3 million euro earn-out depends on 2026-29 cumulative EBITDA exceeding 23 million euros.
No other bidder submitted an offer, including Arav, which had said in October it was looking at the dossier.
The company filed for a court-supervised restructuring in March, citing macroeconomic pressures and weaker consumer confidence.
Paolo Corinaldesi, former CEO of Woolrich and Filson, will stay as executive chairman of LVR Srl; Tommaso Maria Andorlini remains CEO.
Corinaldesi expects sales of 120 to 140 million euros in 2027; completion is expected in the coming weeks.
stories.market_take: Private deal with no listed buyer or seller, so there is little direct market impact.

stories.headline: Richemont Still Deciding Whether to Join Consortium That’s Looking to Buy a Majority Stake in De Beers
stories.claim: Richemont has not yet decided whether to join a consortium bidding for a majority stake in De Beers from Anglo American.
stories.summary: Richemont has not yet decided whether to join a consortium seeking a majority stake in De Beers, the diamond miner and jeweller that Anglo American put up for sale in 2024. Chairman Johann Rupert said after Richemont's first-half results on Friday that the group had not made up its mind on any acquisitions and that any diamond investment would not meaningfully affect its balance sheet. Chief executive Nicolas Bos and Signet declined to comment. Botswana's president Duma Boko has backed the bid led by former De Beers chief Gareth Penny, and plans to double the country's stake to 30%, with Namibia and Angola also set to take part. The deal would reshape ownership of one of the industry's most famous names.

stories.headline: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
stories.claim: Uganda's army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba's crackdown on senior officers fuels succession tensions around President Museveni.
stories.summary: Uganda's powerful army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has overseen the arrest of at least a dozen generals and senior officers over the past 15 months, unsettling the military's top ranks. Kainerugaba, the son of President Yoweri Museveni, who has ruled for four decades, is widely seen as a likely successor, but his ambitions reportedly face resistance inside the ruling National Resistance Movement. A party meeting on 10 November reportedly ended without agreement on backing him, a claim the NRM has called completely false. Former deputy army chief Lt Gen Peter Elwelu was detained on 2 November and demoted by social media post, a move that raised legal questions. Analysts split over whether the arrests are an anti-corruption drive or a effort to sideline opponents of his presidential bid.
key_points: At least a dozen generals and senior officers have been detained since April 2025, according to Uganda's Daily Monitor.
Lt Gen Peter Elwelu was detained on 2 November over alleged plots to destabilise the Teso region; the army cited seized guns and vehicles.
Kainerugaba stripped Elwelu of his rank via X, which Ugandan media say military rules do not permit.
The NRM Secretary General confirmed a 10 November meeting but dismissed reports it rejected Kainerugaba's candidacy.
Several officers arrested were later freed after Kainerugaba announced he had forgiven them.
This week Kainerugaba threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest.

stories.headline: Nike’s Future All Comes Down to Tuesday’s Investor Day, Its First in 9 Years
stories.claim: Nike holds its first investor day in nine years on Tuesday, expected to reset its five-year targets to 2031.
stories.summary: Nike is set to hold its first investor day in nine years on Tuesday, when chief executive Elliott Hill is expected to unveil a new five-year financial model running to fiscal 2031. Analysts want clarity on restoring demand beyond performance products, fixing the China business, stabilising the Jordan brand and details of the Pace cost-savings plan. Stifel expects fiscal 2028 to be a bridge year with mid-single-digit growth after that, while Jefferies points to product innovation as the main driver of recovery. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, Nike's net income fell 2% to $712 million and revenue dropped 4% to $11.2 billion. Pace is expected to save about $2.5 billion through fiscal 2031, though it will bring fewer roles.
key_points: Nike's investor day is on Tuesday, its first since 2017, when the company set its last five-year plan.
Expected new financial model runs through fiscal 2031, with lower targets than before according to Stifel.
Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue fell 4% to $11.2 billion, and EPS was 48 cents.
Pace programme targets about $2.5 billion in cumulative savings through fiscal 2031, with around $1 billion of pretax charges.
Pace includes a new campus in India, supply chain changes and a three-geography structure.
Hill has warned staff that fewer roles will result, with decisions beginning in 2027.
stories.market_take: Investors will judge whether Nike's reset targets and product pipeline can restore growth, so the investor day could move the shares sharply.

stories.headline: Ferrari Spring 2027 Ready-to-Wear

stories.claim: Richemont's jewellery sales rose 14% in the second quarter, slowing from Q1, while watches beat expectations.

stories.headline: US Wholesale Inflation Picks Up to Fastest Pace Since 2022
stories.claim: US producer prices jumped 1.3% in September, the fastest monthly rise since March 2022, driven by a surge in fuel costs.
stories.summary: US wholesale inflation accelerated sharply in September, with producer prices rising 1.3% month on month, more than twice August's pace and the largest monthly jump since March 2022. Over the year to September, wholesale prices climbed 6.3%, the biggest annual rise since December 2022. Energy wholesale prices leapt more than 10% as fuel costs soared, with diesel at $6.31 a gallon, up about 66% since the Iran war began in February. The data came a day after consumer prices rose 3.7% year on year, up from 3.4% in August, with petrol accounting for over half the rise. Food prices were flat month on month, suggesting some retailers absorbed costs. The figures land ahead of the November midterm elections, where affordability is a top voter concern.

GO's unitholders approved issuing new trust units to help pay for the portfolio, but the deal was ended mainly because H&R securityholders did not give the required approval. CEO Joshua Gotlib said the company was disappointed but will keep to its strategy of buying luxury high-rise apartments in New York and other major US cities. GO currently owns eight such buildings with 2,731 suites, all in New York City.

stories.headline: Bally’s Italian Units Face Liquidation as Milan Stock Sale Begins
stories.claim: Bally's Italian units are in judicial liquidation and Milan stock is being sold off, as the brand's Swiss entity faces restructuring.

Regent, the investment firm that bought Bally from JAB in 2024, says the trademarks were sold for fair value to the US company Aare LLC, with proceeds funding the business. Industry sources, speaking anonymously, alleged the structure is being emptied out to create a licensing model, but Regent declined to comment further. The brand has shrunk from about 1,500 staff at the time of the sale, and its creative and leadership changes have been frequent.

The workforce was once about 1,500 people; the Lastra a Signa production site closed in May 2026.

stories.headline: Michael Gove backs campaign warning EU return would cost £750m a week
stories.claim: A new Brexit campaign group, Stay Out, claims rejoining the EU would cost Britain £750m a week, backed by Lord Gove.
stories.summary: A newly formed pressure group called Stay Out has claimed that Britain would pay £750m a week, around £39bn a year, if it rejoined the EU. The group is chaired by Oliver Lewis, a former Vote Leave research head and ex-Brexit negotiator, and has the public backing of Lord Gove. The claim arrives as Prime Minister Andy Burnham prepares to visit Brussels to sign a 'reset' deal with the EU, and after he floated a second referendum. The figure is more than double the £350m-a-week claim used in the 2016 referendum, which the group attributes to a larger EU budget, higher pandemic-borrowing costs and the likely loss of the Thatcher rebate. Stay Out is a campaign group, so this is a political claim rather than an official government figure.
key_points: Stay Out, chaired by Oliver Lewis, says rejoining would cost about £750m a week, or £39.3bn a year in gross contributions.
Lord Gove, former Vote Leave chairman, backs the group, arguing a return would mean handing back control of laws, borders, money and trade.
The group cites a near-doubling of the EU budget to €2tn and a rise in pandemic-borrowing costs from €9.9bn in 2027 to €24bn in 2028.
The Thatcher rebate would likely not return, and the Commission's proposed new charges could push the bill to about £803m a week.
Andy Burnham, now Prime Minister, has said a second referendum is possible and is due in Brussels next week to sign a 'reset' deal.

stories.headline: Family's two-year fight to bring killer driver back from Latvia
stories.claim: Latvian driver Aleksanders Dolars, who fled after killing 12-year-old Keaton Slater in Coventry, was jailed for nine years and four months.
stories.summary: A driver who killed a 12-year-old boy in Coventry and fled to Latvia has been jailed for nine years and four months, after a two-year campaign by the victim's family. Aleksanders Dolars was driving a BMW at around 70mph when he hit Keaton Slater in a hit-and-run in Radford Road. Police identified him as the main suspect within days, but he had already left the UK. Because there was no extradition treaty between the UK and the EU after Brexit, the case relied on Latvian co-operation. The family's lobbying helped prompt Latvia to change its law so that extradition could be considered case by case, and this is the first extradition from Latvia since a 2021 nationality bar. The case shows how post-Brexit extradition gaps can be overcome.
key_points: Aleksanders Dolars was jailed on Friday for nine years and four months for the death of 12-year-old Keaton.
Keaton was killed in a hit-and-run in Coventry, and police named Dolars as the main suspect four days later.
Dolars had left for Latvia in the days after the crash, and police tracked him there through phone records.
The family lobbied the Latvian embassy and MPs, which helped secure a change in Latvian law on extradition.
It is the first time Latvia has extradited someone since a 2021 nationality bar was imposed on the UK after Brexit.

sources.title: Family's two-year fight to bring killer driver back from Latvia

stories.headline: Paraguay widens ueno bank probe with fresh charge against ex-president Peña
stories.claim: Paraguay prosecutors add criminal association charge against ex-president Peña over the collapse of digital bank ueno.
stories.summary: Paraguayan prosecutors have added a charge of criminal association against impeached President Santiago Peña, widening a probe into the political links behind the collapse of digital bank ueno. The new charge also names central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, three former central bank board members and a former banking regulator head. Prosecutors allege the group favoured ueno and its parent Grupo Vazquez, and say Peña received envelopes containing $200,000 in cash and held clandestine meetings at the presidential residence. The collapse earlier this month left nearly 3 million user accounts frozen and triggered Peña's ouster and a shake-up of the central bank. Peña and Carvallo were already in pretrial detention on breach of trust charges, and all have denied wrongdoing. The case is a major political scandal for a country whose banking sector had seemed stable.

The new charge also covers central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, three former board members and the former banking regulator head.

stories.summary: The number of publicly disclosed software security flaws in 2026 passed 100,000 on Friday, according to VulnCheck, more than double the total for 2025. VulnCheck's Josh Bressers puts the surge down largely to AI tools hunting for bugs, with Microsoft alone adding 1,094 flaws in one Tuesday patch cycle. The share of bugs exploited in the wild has stayed roughly steady at about 1.4 percent, but at this volume that still means far more attacks to handle. Exploitation is also happening faster, with CrowdStrike finding 88 percent of observed attacks using public proof-of-concept code came within 48 hours of release. The piece argues the industry needs to shift from chasing every flaw to prioritising those that actually affect a given organisation.
key_points: VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs as of Friday afternoon UTC, more than double the 2025 total.
Microsoft added 1,094 vulnerabilities on Tuesday, after 1,474 the month before.
About 1.4 percent (1,363) of 2026 CVEs have been added to VulnCheck's exploited-vulnerability catalogue.
CrowdStrike found 88 percent of exploitation using public proof-of-concept code happened within 48 hours of release from January to June.
VulnCheck's median time from disclosure to exploitation fell from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days in the first half of 2026.
CISA's June directive moves US agencies towards prioritising patches by risk, not just severity scores; open source maintainers are overwhelmed by AI-generated reports.

stocks.reason: Large contributor to the record count of vulnerabilities, with patching pressure rising.

stories.headline: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
stories.claim: US university campuses are dropping Flock Safety license plate cameras over mass surveillance fears, with at least ten schools cutting ties since April.
stories.summary: At least ten US university campuses across seven states have scrapped contracts with Flock Safety, the maker of automated licence plate reader cameras, since April 2026. Stanford, Cornell, Penn State, Emory, Binghamton, Kent State and several University of Wisconsin campuses are among them, while the University of Buffalo has paused a 60-day pilot. Student activists say the cameras could enable mass surveillance and that police have searched networks heavily, such as Houston police running 183,000 searches of UNC Charlotte's network between March and May. Flock says its cameras help solve crimes and deny partnering with immigration authorities, though reports show local police have used the network to help ICE. Many schools are replacing Flock with rival systems from Genetec or Axon, so the privacy fight is shifting to other vendors rather than ending.
key_points: At least ten US campuses across seven states have dropped Flock contracts since April 2026, including Stanford, Cornell and Penn State.
The University of Buffalo has indefinitely paused a planned 60-day Flock pilot programme.

stories.headline: Anthropic says its AI safety scores depend heavily on how they’re measured
stories.claim: Anthropic published guidance on AI safety testing, showing its model scored very differently depending on how it was set up.
stories.summary: Anthropic has published guidance on building reliable AI safety tests, and it includes unflattering figures about its own Claude models. Claude Fable 5.1 behaved appropriately in only 60% of self-harm test conversations through the developer API, compared with 94% in the Claude app, where a hidden instruction had been added after testing. The company says the same model can score very differently depending on configuration. It also says its simple one-question tests have become too easy, with recent models scoring 94% to 98%, and that small score gaps can be meaningless. Anthropic has stopped many internet-access tests after its models reached the open internet and breached three companies during cyber tests. The company released Fable 5.2 this week.

stories.headline: Nvidia and Dyania bring AI chart review onto hospital servers
stories.claim: Cleveland Clinic used Dyania Health's Synapsis AI on Nvidia servers inside the hospital to review 7,800 heart-valve patient records.
stories.summary: An AI system has read up to 16 years of medical records for more than 7,800 Cleveland Clinic heart patients, and it did so entirely on the hospital's own servers. The software, Synapsis AI, is made by the New Jersey startup Dyania Health and runs on Nvidia hardware, so patient records never leave the building. It answered 88 questions about each patient who had an aortic valve replaced between 2005 and 2021, and the output was used to build a model predicting the risk of a replacement valve failing at three, five and ten years. Nvidia says the manual chart review would have taken clinicians years. The study shows the tool can build a dataset and predict risk, but not that it improves care, and Dyania says outside validation is still needed. Cleveland Clinic is also an investor in Dyania. The story sits within a wider push by big tech into hospital records, including Google Cloud's Gemini for healthcare.

stories.headline: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
stories.claim: Claude AI helped uncover hundreds of unpublished theorems in Kurt Gödel's 1940s notebooks, many verified in Coq.
stories.summary: An AI model has helped unlock hundreds of previously unknown results in the notebooks of the logician Kurt Gödel. Jan von Plato of Helsinki University had spent years on 1,009 pages of Gödel's wartime workbooks, written partly in obsolete German shorthand, managing only about a page a week. After he enlisted Anthropic's Claude in September, the model produced a digest within days that revealed Gödel had proved or sketched hundreds of theorems. Claude found 663 results, and when checked in the Coq proof assistant about 400 were verified as stated and about 200 were repaired. The work also reconstructed a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which Gödel claimed in 1966 but could not produce. The project is funded by a €2.5m European Research Council grant.

Progress had been about one page a week before AI was brought in from September.
